hero.title: The 60-Second Read · Ahmed
hero.description: Our call written as a brief: the bet before, what happened after, the moment it clicked, and one move.
hero.title_html: What I got right, where I was wrong, and what to do about it.
hero.lead_html: Our call, written as a brief: what I expected walking in, what actually happened, and one concrete move. Sixty seconds, four short reads. No math on this page; the scoring is one click down, closed until you ask.

bet.sub: The bet I filed before the call, from your note and your public work. Written down first so it could be scored honestly after.

cards.label: Who you are
cards.head: An old founder friend, back in town.
cards.body_html: You reached out first: back in NYC, saw my post, wanted to catch up. I filed it as a warm reconnect, not a business call.

cards.label: What you want
cards.head: To show me the media pitch.
cards.body_html: I bet your live fire was the proposal to sell media companies context for AI, and that you'd want my honest read on it.

cards.label: What I want
cards.head: To leave one useful thing.
cards.body_html: Not to pitch. Offer to pressure-test that proposal the way I'd pressure-test a launch, and see if anything real overlapped.

outcome.sub: What actually happened, scored against that bet. The half a normal brief never fills in.

cards.label: What happened
cards.head: You named the overlap before I could.
cards.body_html: <q>We're targeting a very similar set of customers and we're targeting a very similar set of problems.</q> Then you sketched the deal on the spot: run this read on your customers' sales calls, under your name.

cards.label: Where I was wrong
cards.head: The media pitch wasn't the main event.
cards.body_html: I bet it was your live fire. You demoted it yourself: <q>a separate side project, the main company is Polyform.</q> The real heat was your customers' need, not your product. That's the miss, kept on purpose.

cards.label: What to do
cards.head: Follow your pull, not my plan.
cards.body_html: You asked about pricing without me raising it. So the next step isn't a pitch from me; it's the one report you already sketched.

spark.sub: One line on the call snapped the two companies into one picture. Your line, not mine.
spark.quote: …what you're doing for a human being. How would I give them your decision science?
spark.quote_attrib: you, on the Jul 22 call, connecting your context-not-content pitch to this work
spark.body_html: You'd spent years standardizing the context a company's data sits in. I'd been standardizing the context a person decides in. When you said that line, they collapsed into one picture: the same architecture, built from opposite ends. And it rhymed with where you started, tracking objects at Raytheon so the human only had to make the final call. The idea was already yours; the call just lit it.

move.sub: One move, not a menu. Everything above is just the demo.
move.panel_html: First: yes to the Robert intro you offered, whenever it's easy. Then the one move: pick one customer with a lot of sales calls. The first report runs on me, so it costs you nothing to see. If it lands, we put a fixed per-customer number on it the moment we pick who. One customer, their existing timeline export, your name on the report.

math.summary_label: Show the work · the scoring behind the read
math.summary_html: You standardize what a company's activity means; this is the same trick pointed at a conversation. Before the call I wrote each expectation down, line by line, and the call itself settled them. A read that turns out wrong is kept, not smoothed over; the wrong lines are where the next read gets sharper. Open only if you want the receipt.
